aiExplanation: This is a straightforward **brute force** approach: for every possible starting index `i`, it walks forward through every ending index `j`, keeping a `Set` of the values seen so far in the subarray `nums[i..j]`. Because a `Set` only stores unique values, `set.size` is exactly the number of **distinct elements** in that subarray, so the code adds `set.size * set.size` (the distinct count squared) to the running total `res` for every subarray. After checking all `O(n^2)` subarrays it returns `res`. The logic is correct, but it never applies the required modulo `10^9 + 7`, so for large inputs the result overflows or does not match the expected answer, which is why this attempt **failed**.

author: Vitor
aiExplanation: This is the same **brute force** idea as before, with the missing modulo fixed: for every starting index `i`, it expands the subarray one element at a time by moving `j` forward, adding each value to a `Set` so that `set.size` gives the number of **distinct elements** in `nums[i..j]`. For each subarray it adds the square of that distinct count to `res`, wrapping with `% mod` where `mod` is `10^9 + 7` so the number stays in range. The answer is now correct, but because it still visits every one of the `O(n^2)` subarrays and does `Set` work for each, it is too slow for the largest inputs and results in **Time Limit Exceeded**.

author: Leetcode
notes: I had seen some possible solutions for this the day before, and I already knew attempting to get an accepted on this one was not worth it.
aiExplanation: This solution sweeps through the array once, maintaining `cur` as the sum of **(distinct count)²** over all subarrays that end at the current index `i`. The key insight is that when `A[i]` arrives, it only becomes a *new* distinct value for subarrays that start after its previous occurrence (tracked in the `seen` map), i.e. every start index from `j` to `i`; for those subarrays the distinct count `d` grows by one, so their squared contribution changes by `(d+1)² - d² = 2d + 1`. A **Binary Indexed Tree** (`BIT`) with two internal arrays supports both *range add* and *range sum*, and it stores the current distinct count for every possible start index, so `bit.query(j, i)` returns the sum of all those `d` values in `O(log n)`. The code then updates `cur` by `2 * sum + (i - j + 1)`, adds `cur` into the global answer `res`, increments the range `[j, i]` by one in the tree, and records `i` as the latest position of `A[i]`. Everything is done with `BigInt` and reduced modulo `1000000007` to avoid overflow, giving an overall `O(n log n)` algorithm.
